title: "Useful GitHub: LUTO2 and the hard problem of choosing land uses"
description: "Australia's open LUTO2 model shows what spatial land-use optimisation looks like when food, carbon, biodiversity, water and economics have to occupy the same map."

Land-use modelling becomes interesting when two desirable things want the same hectare.

A parcel may produce food, store carbon, support biodiversity, provide water benefits or earn income under another land use. National targets add another layer: the resulting landscape still has to satisfy demands that operate well beyond the parcel itself. Once those objectives interact, drawing a future land-use map becomes an optimisation problem rather than a colouring exercise.

That is what makes the public LUTO2 repository worth examining.

LUTO2, the Land-Use Trade-Offs Model Version 2.0, is an integrated land-systems model for Australia developed through Deakin University and Climateworks Centre, with research contributions from CSIRO. The repository describes the model's task as finding spatial arrangements of land use and management through time while accounting for objectives including climate, biodiversity, economic activity, food production and water security. It is released under the GNU GPL v3 licence.

The interesting part is not simply that the code is open. It is the architecture of the problem.

The repository separates agricultural and non-agricultural economics, with modules for costs, revenues, greenhouse gases, biodiversity, water, production quantities and land-use transitions. A solver layer then represents decision variables, constraints and the objective passed to Gurobi. Outputs feed into a reporting system with maps and other visualisations. This separation is useful because it makes explicit something that is often hidden in integrated models: a land-use result is produced by several linked accounting systems, not by a single equation.

LUTO2 also has a long horizon. Its documentation says the current version extends from 2010 to 2100 and includes additional land-use options, management solutions, sustainability indicators and demand-side measures compared with the original LUTO model. The modelling approach has also been informed by stakeholder consultation.

There are practical lessons here for researchers building smaller spatial models.

First, **keep the accounting modules separable**. Carbon, biodiversity, water and farm economics may ultimately enter one decision problem, but keeping their calculations distinct makes auditing easier. If an output looks strange, a researcher can ask whether the problem originates in the emissions calculation, a transition cost, a land constraint or the optimiser itself.

Second, **treat infeasibility as information**. The repository contains explicit tools for diagnosing years in which model constraints cannot jointly be satisfied. That is more than a programming convenience. In policy modelling, an infeasible scenario can be substantively meaningful. Targets may compete for the same finite land, or transition rules may prevent the landscape from reaching a requested configuration. A model should help explain that conflict rather than merely fail.

Third, **reporting belongs inside the modelling system**. LUTO2 contains a substantial reporting layer rather than treating visualisation as an afterthought. Spatial models produce too much information for a single national total to be sufficient. Maps, trajectories and disaggregated indicators are part of understanding the solution.

The repository also reveals the limits of "open source" as a synonym for "immediately reproducible." LUTO2's README says its input database is roughly 40 GB and contains sensitive data that must be requested from the development team. It requires substantial computing resources, Python 3.10 or later according to the setup guidance, and the commercial Gurobi optimiser, although academic licences are available. The public code therefore provides transparency about model structure without making every published run frictionless to reproduce.

That distinction matters. Reproducibility has layers: open code, accessible inputs, documented environments, solver availability and sufficient computing resources. A repository can be excellent on some dimensions and constrained on others.

LUTO2 is useful partly because of its scale, but the more transferable lesson is architectural. Serious land-use modelling requires a visible chain from assumptions, to sectoral calculations, to constraints, to spatial choices, to outputs that a researcher can interrogate.

The map at the end is only the last step.
